strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem: forecasting multivariate biomedical trajectories under specified conditions and time horizons, with interpretable controls over individual variables.
CLEF is simple and modular. Its multiplicative prediction head can be combined with Transformer, xLSTM, and frozen MOMENT encoders, and its variable-aligned outputs make manual edits straightforward.

The evaluation spans cellular trajectories and two large clinical datasets, includes immediate and delayed prediction, and examines distribution shift using SPECTRA. Figure 4 and Table 2 provide evidence of forecasting improvements over the implemented neural baselines, particularly for Transformer and xLSTM under distribution shift.
weaknesses: The central counterfactual and causal-consistency claims are not established. CLEF minimizes observational prediction loss without specifying causal identification assumptions or addressing confounding. Clinical conditions are diagnosis codes, rather than administered treatments (Appendix A.2). Predicting laboratory results conditional on a diagnosis does not identify the effects of medication, surgery, or changing intervention timing. Preserving historical inputs also does not establish causal validity.

WOT-CF does not provide validated interventional ground truth. Appendix A.1 constructs alternative futures by independently sampling continuations from the same observational optimal-transport model, then retrospectively assigning transcription-factor conditions through differential expression. This does not demonstrate that activating the assigned factor causes the sampled continuation. Moreover, test trajectories share prefixes with training or validation trajectories, and the protocol does not establish that test conditions are unseen; the scope of the claimed zero-shot generalization is therefore limited.

The architectural contribution is primarily a multiplicative forecasting parameterization: the predicted value equals the latest observation times a learned factor. Comparisons against additive residual heads and equally conditioned direct horizon predictors are needed to establish the value of the proposed concepts. The parameterization also forces any variable whose latest value is zero to remain zero, regardless of the condition, while the ratio-based concept is undefined at zero. This is particularly relevant to the log-normalized gene-expression data, and no remedy is described.

The claimed temporal and structural control is insufficiently specified and evaluated. Definition 3.1 uses the same time for intervention occurrence and outcome prediction, conflating delayed intervention with prediction at a longer horizon. The model lacks an explicit mechanism guaranteeing preservation of unaffected future variables, and aggregate MAE/RMSE do not test this property. Separate intervention and outcome times, preservation metrics, and controlled delayed-effect experiments are needed.

Baseline coverage and implementation details do not support the broad state-of-the-art claims. The experiments mainly compare encoder variants rather than established longitudinal treatment-effect methods or the cited conditional generation systems. It is unclear whether delayed baselines receive equivalent horizon information and direct-prediction training. VAR produces catastrophic errors on clinical data, warranting investigation of fitting and stabilization. Persistence and VAR outperform CLEF on delayed WOT prediction, yet neither appears in the WOT-CF evaluation, where they would be especially informative.

The clinical case studies do not validate treatment recommendations or symptom reversal. Manually lowering glucose and measuring similarity to non-diabetic patients partly builds the desired result into the evaluation. Indirect effects are compared with observed trajectories rather than an otherwise identical unedited model rollout, so prediction error can be mistaken for intervention effects. Cohort construction also identifies ICD-9 category 250 as equivalent to type 1 diabetes, although it includes other diabetes types. Additionally, Figures 7 and 14 label ratios as observed/CLEF while interpreting ratios below one as decreases in CLEF values; that direction requires correction or clarification.

Reproducibility and uncertainty reporting are incomplete. The manuscript mentions a GitHub repository without providing an identifiable link, and omits important details about missing-value handling, normalization, training-pair and horizon sampling, baseline conditioning, and the number of runs underlying error bars. The WOT split is described as random in figure captions but start-cluster-based in Appendix A.1. These omissions make the reported gains difficult to independently assess.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem: condition- and time-dependent prediction of multivariate biomedical trajectories with user-controlled edits.

CLEF is simple and modular, combining interchangeable sequence encoders with a multiplicative prediction head. Experiments across Transformer, xLSTM, and MOMENT provide evidence of its utility as a forecasting inductive bias.

Evaluation includes cellular trajectories, two substantial patient datasets, and SPECTRA distribution-shift experiments. The reported improvements over corresponding neural baselines, particularly under patient distribution shifts, are promising.
weaknesses: The central counterfactual interpretation is unsupported. Training minimizes observational prediction error without stating causal identification assumptions or addressing confounding. Patient conditions are diagnosis codes, rather than assigned treatments. Conditioning on a diagnosis or editing a predicted laboratory value does not establish the effect of a clinical intervention; preserving historical inputs alone does not ensure causal consistency.

WOT-CF does not provide validated intervention counterfactuals. Appendix A.1 constructs alternative futures by independently sampling continuations from an optimal-transport model, then infers transcription-factor conditions retrospectively from source and destination cell groups. These labels incorporate information about the outcome rather than specifying an experimentally controlled perturbation. Consequently, prediction accuracy on these trajectories cannot establish accurate transcription-factor intervention effects.

The claimed localized editing guarantees exceed the architecture and evaluation. Equations (1)–(2) contain no explicit mechanism enforcing preservation of unaffected variables, and aggregate MAE/RMSE do not measure edit locality or preservation. The formulation also uses the requested time as both intervention time and prediction time, without separately modeling intervention onset and elapsed response time.

The multiplicative decoder has an important unaddressed limitation: when an input coordinate is zero, its prediction must remain zero for every condition and horizon. This is particularly consequential for sparse gene-expression data, where activation from zero is biologically meaningful. The ratio-based concept definition is likewise undefined at zero, and no handling of this issue is described.

Comparisons do not adequately isolate the contribution. Missing controls include an additive residual prediction head, a condition-ablated model, and a directly horizon-conditioned forecasting baseline with matched inputs and training. Relevant longitudinal treatment-effect methods are also absent. SimpleLinear is effectively a persistence predictor, yet it and VAR outperform the neural methods on delayed WOT prediction; these simple baselines are omitted from the WOT-CF comparison.

The zero-shot claim is overstated. WOT-CF places original trajectories in training or validation and their alternative continuations in testing, sharing identical prefixes. This tests prediction of alternative sampled futures, but does not demonstrate generalization to unseen intervention identities or independent cellular starting histories.

The clinical case studies do not validate treatment recommendations or physiological causal effects. Manually lowering glucose and observing greater similarity to healthy patients is insufficient without untreated model rollouts, simple editing controls, or intervention outcomes. Cross-variable effects require clarification because the immediate decoder is coordinatewise. Additionally, Appendix A.2 treats ICD-9 code 250 as equivalent to type 1 diabetes, although that category includes other diabetes types, undermining cohort specificity.

Important reproducibility details are missing or unclear, including missing-value processing, feature scaling, training horizon sampling, baseline conditioning and rollout procedures, and the number of runs and meaning of error bars. These omissions make the unusually unstable VAR results and aggregate errors across heterogeneous laboratory measurements difficult to assess.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem: conditioning multivariate biomedical forecasts on both a desired condition and a future time, with interpretable variable-level controls.

CLEF is simple and modular. Its multiplicative prediction mechanism can be combined with different sequence encoders, and experiments demonstrate improvements across Transformer, xLSTM, and frozen MOMENT representations.

The evaluation includes substantial patient datasets, simulated cellular trajectories, multiple forecast horizons, and challenging SPECTRA splits. The generalization improvements in Appendix Table 2 provide concrete evidence that the proposed parameterization can improve predictive performance.
weaknesses: The central causal claims are unsupported. Training minimizes observational prediction error, and patient conditions are diagnosis codes rather than administered interventions. No identification assumptions or confounding adjustment establish that changing these inputs estimates treatment effects. Preserving historical inputs does not establish causal consistency or justify claims about discovering beneficial clinical interventions.

WOT-CF does not provide validated interventional counterfactuals. Appendix A.1 constructs alternative futures by independently sampling from the same optimal-transport process, then infers transcription-factor conditions retrospectively from observed transitions. This evaluates prediction with outcome-derived labels, not the effect of experimentally changing a transcription factor. Furthermore, shared prefixes between training originals and test alternatives make this different from demonstrating generalization to unseen interventions.

The formulation does not substantiate several advertised editing capabilities. Intervention time and outcome time are represented by the same future coordinate, so delayed intervention is not separated from delayed response. There is also no explicit constraint enforcing preservation of unaffected variables, nor an evaluation measuring edit localization or cross-variable causal consistency.

Baseline comparisons and ablations do not isolate the contribution. SimpleLinear is effectively persistence, while a learned additive residual predictor and a matched direct multi-horizon conditional predictor are missing. Condition-removal and time-removal ablations are also needed. SimpleLinear and VAR outperform the neural models on delayed WOT prediction, but these strong simple baselines are omitted from WOT-CF evaluation. Exploding VAR errors on patient data further weaken the comparisons.

The multiplicative decoder has an important unaddressed limitation: a variable whose last observed value is zero must remain zero at the predicted time, regardless of condition. This matters for sparse gene-expression data. The ratio-based concept definition is also undefined at zero, and the manuscript does not explain how preprocessing resolves this issue.

The clinical case study is insufficient to validate physiological effects. Manually halving glucose and measuring similarity to healthy controls partly builds the desired result into the intervention; it does not establish a feasible treatment or its downstream effects. Cohorts are small, and Appendix A.2 treats ICD-9 category 250 as equivalent to type 1 diabetes, although that category includes multiple diabetes types. These issues weaken the clinical interpretation.

Reproducibility and evaluation details are incomplete: the manuscript references a GitHub repository without providing a usable link, and does not sufficiently specify missing-value handling, variable scaling, horizon sampling, baseline conditioning and rollout procedures, or the repetitions underlying uncertainty estimates. Overall, the forecasting results are promising, but the evidence does not support the paper's principal counterfactual and clinical claims at the acceptance threshold.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: predicting multivariate biological and clinical trajectories under conditions specified at different future times.
CLEF is a simple, modular architecture that can augment different sequence encoders. The multiplicative prediction mechanism provides an interpretable per-variable representation of relative change.

The evaluation is broad, covering cellular trajectories, two large clinical datasets, and established synthetic and semi-synthetic counterfactual benchmarks. Multiple seeds, confidence intervals, and increasingly dissimilar train/test splits are useful components.

The reported improvements over corresponding neural baselines, particularly for delayed prediction and some strongly confounded simulation settings, suggest that the proposed parameterization provides a useful forecasting inductive bias.
weaknesses: The causal justification is unsound. Section 3.3 argues that separately encoding historical covariates and the next treatment produces treatment-invariant representations. Covariates can remain highly predictive of treatment despite separate encoders, and the final concepts explicitly incorporate treatment. Assumption 3.4 largely assumes the desired conditional-mean estimation property; predictive improvements without balancing losses do not demonstrate this assumption or representation balance, contrary to Section 5.4.

The new datasets do not establish the advertised intervention capabilities. In eICU and MIMIC-IV, conditions are diagnosis codes aligned with laboratory measurements, rather than administered treatments. In WOT, transcription-factor conditions are inferred retrospectively from expression differences between source and destination cell groups. These setups support conditional prediction, but do not validate effects of administering a particular intervention at a chosen time. The distinction is especially consequential for the delayed-intervention claims.

WOT-CF does not provide validated interventional counterfactual ground truth. Appendix C.1 constructs alternative trajectories by independently resampling future states from the same optimal-transport process after a shared prefix, with conditions inferred afterward. This does not establish that changing the inferred transcription factor causes the alternative trajectory. Furthermore, original trajectories appear in training or validation while their shared-prefix alternatives appear in testing; this evaluates a narrower form of generalization than unseen-patient or unseen-intervention zero-shot prediction.

The experiments do not adequately isolate the methodological contribution. Temporal concepts are predicted multiplicative factors, while SimpleLinear with all-one concepts is simply persistence. Missing comparisons include matched direct-horizon predictors with additive residual heads, learned linear predictors, and condition/time ablations. These are needed to distinguish benefits of the multiplicative parameterization from persistence bias and direct forecasting. SimpleLinear and VAR outperform CLEF on delayed WOT prediction, and the extremely unstable clinical VAR results weaken that comparison.

The claimed preservation of unaffected variables is neither guaranteed nor directly evaluated. Equation 3 can modify every variable, with no mask or constraint enforcing preservation. Forecasting only future values trivially leaves the supplied history unchanged. Aggregate MAE/RMSE does not demonstrate selective editing, absence of pre-intervention effects, or consistency across separately queried future times.

The multiplicative decoder has an important unaddressed expressivity limitation: a variable whose latest value is zero must remain zero in every direct prediction, regardless of history or condition. Definition 3.2 also divides by potentially zero observations. This is particularly relevant to sparse gene-expression data and standardized outcomes. The paper needs an explicit treatment of zeros and near-zero values and evidence that this restriction does not drive its results.

The diabetes case study does not substantiate discovery of clinical interventions. Directly halving a predicted glucose-related factor and observing greater similarity to selected controls is not evidence of an achievable treatment effect; subsequent correlated changes likewise do not establish causality. Cohort definitions also need correction or clarification: ICD-9 category 250 is not specific to type 1 diabetes, and the listed control exclusions omit E10. With only 59 and 25 designated T1D patients, these concerns materially weaken the clinical conclusions.

strengths: The problem is relevant: conditional forecasting with explicit temporal control has useful applications in biological and clinical sequence modeling.
CLEF is simple and modular. Its multiplicative prediction mechanism can be incorporated into different sequence encoders and existing counterfactual prediction architectures.

The experiments provide meaningful evidence of predictive improvements across multiple encoders, clinical datasets, and synthetic counterfactual benchmarks. Evaluation includes multiple seeds, distribution-shift splits, and comparisons with CRN and Causal Transformer.
weaknesses: The causal justification is unsound. Section 3.3 claims that independently encoding historical covariates and treatment produces treatment-invariant representations, but historical covariates can remain strongly predictive of treatment under confounding. Assumption 3.4 largely assumes the desired conditional-mean estimation property. Improved prediction error without a balancing loss does not demonstrate representation balance or isolation of causal effects, contrary to Section 5.4.

The central editing claims exceed what the architecture and evaluation establish. Predicting a future endpoint preserves the supplied history trivially, while Equations 2–3 contain no explicit mechanism ensuring that unaffected variables remain unchanged. Aggregate MAE does not measure edit locality. Moreover, treatment time and outcome measurement time are effectively coupled, so the experiments do not convincingly establish control over intervention timing independently of forecast horizon.

The multiplicative decoder has an important unaddressed limitation: when a variable's latest value is zero, its prediction must remain zero regardless of history, condition, or horizon. The ratio-based concept is also undefined at zero, and GELU restricts the attainable negative ratios. These issues matter for sparse gene-expression measurements and standardized outcomes, yet the paper provides no analysis or mitigation.

The new biological benchmarks do not establish interventional counterfactual accuracy. Appendix C.1 assigns transcription-factor conditions retrospectively from observed state transitions; WOT-CF independently samples alternative continuations from an optimal-transport model rather than simulating an explicit transcription-factor intervention. Consequently, performance measures prediction of constructed alternative trajectories, not validated causal responses. Its zero-shot split also shares initial trajectory segments with training examples and does not establish generalization to unseen interventions.

Novelty and experimental attribution remain insufficient. The core method is a learned, condition-dependent multiplicative forecast relative to the latest observation. Missing comparisons with additive residual predictors and matched direct, horizon-conditioned predictors leave unclear whether gains require the proposed temporal concepts. SimpleLinear is a persistence predictor rather than a learned linear baseline; persistence and VAR outperform the neural models on delayed WOT forecasting. The reported numerical explosion of clinical VAR forecasts further weakens that comparison.

The clinical case study does not validate treatment effects or clinical benefit. Conditions in the clinical benchmarks are diagnosis codes, whereas the case study manually changes predicted glucose or WBC values without specifying a treatment that causes those changes. Greater similarity to selected controls cannot establish physiological correctness of downstream effects. Cohort construction is also problematic: ICD-9 category 250 is not specific to type 1 diabetes, and the listed control exclusions do not explicitly exclude E10. These issues undermine the interpretation of the small cohorts as evidence for discovering beneficial interventions.

Important reproducibility details remain unclear, including handling of asynchronous or missing clinical measurements, normalization and aggregation across lab tests with different units, delayed-horizon training and baseline conditioning, and incorporation of treatment history into the main architecture. The available implementation descriptions and hyperparameter lists do not resolve these ambiguities.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: condition-dependent prediction of multivariate biological and clinical trajectories at user-selected future times.
CLEF is simple and modular. Its multiplicative prediction head can be integrated with different sequence encoders, including existing counterfactual prediction architectures.

The empirical study covers several domains, multiple encoders, increasingly challenging patient splits, and synthetic counterfactual benchmarks. Results across three or five seeds provide concrete evidence of predictive improvements, particularly under distribution shift and in some confounded simulation settings.
The appendix provides useful dataset construction details, hyperparameter settings, and additional evaluations.
weaknesses: The causal justification is unsound as stated. Encoding historical covariates and treatment separately does not make representations treatment-invariant: covariates can remain strongly predictive of treatment assignment. Assumption 3.4 effectively assumes successful conditional-mean estimation, and improved counterfactual RMSE does not demonstrate representation balance or isolation of causal effects, contrary to Sections 3.3 and 5.4.

The proposed benchmarks do not establish several central intervention claims. Patient conditions are diagnosis codes rather than administered treatments. In WOT, transcription-factor conditions are inferred retrospectively from source and destination cell groups; WOT-CF independently resamples continuations rather than simulating an explicitly manipulated transcription factor. These evaluations support conditional prediction more directly than causal intervention modeling. Sharing prefixes with training trajectories also makes the claimed zero-shot setting narrower than generalization to unseen interventions or patients.

The novelty and source of improvement are insufficiently isolated. The central mechanism is a learned multiplicative forecast relative to the last observation. Comparisons against additive residual prediction, learned linear models, and matched direct multi-horizon predictors are needed to distinguish benefits of this parameterization from the proposed temporal-concept interpretation. SimpleLinear is actually a persistence predictor, and it outperforms neural models on delayed WOT prediction.

The claimed preservation of unaffected variables is neither enforced nor directly evaluated. Equation 3 can change every coordinate; there is no explicit mask or invariance constraint. Preserving historical inputs is standard in forecasting, while aggregate MAE and RMSE do not measure selective editing or condition adherence. Likewise, querying a future timestamp alone does not demonstrate correct scheduling of an intervention independently of its subsequent effects.

The multiplicative decoder has an important unaddressed expressivity limitation: if a variable's latest value is zero, its prediction must remain zero regardless of the history or condition. The temporal-concept ratio is also undefined at zero. This is particularly relevant to sparse gene-expression measurements. GELU additionally restricts attainable negative multipliers, which matters for sign changes in standardized outcomes.

The clinical case study overinterprets associative simulations. Manually reducing glucose and observing greater similarity to controls does not identify a clinical intervention or validate its causal downstream effects. Cohort construction also contains a substantive concern: ICD-9 category 250 includes multiple diabetes types and is not equivalent to type 1 diabetes code E10; the listed control exclusions omit E10. These issues weaken the clinical conclusions.

Several comparisons leave uncertainty about competitiveness. The cited controllable diffusion approaches are not directly benchmarked, VAR exhibits extreme numerical instability, and the zero-shot WOT evaluation omits the persistence baseline despite its strong ordinary WOT performance. Consequently, the reported percentage gains do not establish superiority over sufficiently strong alternatives.

strengths: CLEF offers a simple, modular multiplicative decoder that can be integrated with several sequence encoders with little additional parameter or computational overhead. Its variable-wise factors provide a straightforward interface for editing predictions.

The empirical evaluation is broad, covering biological, clinical, and sales data, multiple encoders, synthetic counterfactual benchmarks, and challenging patient-distribution splits. Multiple seeds, uncertainty estimates, and decoder ablations strengthen the experimental evidence.

There are meaningful predictive improvements over matched non-CLEF models, particularly in delayed cellular forecasting and patient-distribution generalization. The synthetic experiments also provide useful evidence of improved counterfactual prediction under stronger confounding.
weaknesses: The central claim that CLEF intrinsically learns balanced representations is not justified. Encoding covariates and treatment separately does not make covariate representations independent of treatment assignment when covariates contain confounders; the concept representation also explicitly incorporates treatment. Assumption 3.4 assumes the desired conditional-mean approximation rather than establishing it. Tables 10–12 do not resolve this: higher classifier BCE alone does not demonstrate invariance without a well-trained independent probe and an appropriate reference, and the tables omit the no-balancing-loss models underlying the strongest claim.

The WOT-CF construction does not establish ground-truth intervention counterfactuals. Appendix C.1 samples alternative continuations from the same optimal-transport process and assigns transcription-factor conditions retrospectively from expression differences between cell groups. This supports conditional prediction of alternative sampled paths, but does not identify the effect of experimentally activating a transcription factor. Original and alternative trajectories also share prefixes across training and testing, and the split does not establish held-out intervention identities. The zero-shot counterfactual claims substantially exceed this evidence.

The proposed temporal concepts are essentially predicted per-variable multiplicative factors. The evaluation lacks the most informative controls for this inductive bias: additive residual prediction, a learned affine decoder, and otherwise matched direct horizon-conditioned forecasting. The SimpleLinear ablation is persistence, not a fitted linear forecaster. Improvements over selected encoder heads therefore do not establish that concept learning, rather than anchoring predictions to the latest observation, explains the gains. Moreover, Table 9 already includes non-CLEF direct predictions, weakening claims that one-step delayed forecasting is unique to CLEF.

The advertised control over timing and scope is stronger than the formulation supports. Equations 2–3 contain no explicit mask or constraint that forces unaffected variables to remain unchanged; Table 5 reports prediction error rather than establishing preservation. Historical inputs remain unchanged because the model predicts future values. Intervention and measurement times are also tied together, so the experiments do not independently establish control over intervention onset and subsequent response timing.

The clinical case study does not validate actionable treatment effects. Conditions in the patient datasets are diagnosis codes, while the case study directly scales glucose or WBC predictions and evaluates resemblance to comparison patients. Such similarity cannot establish physiological realism or the causal consequences of a clinical intervention. Cohort construction is also questionable: ICD-9 category 250 includes both diabetes types and is not equivalent to type-1-specific E10, while the stated control exclusions omit E10 itself. These issues weaken the interpretation of the small T1D cohorts.

The decoder has important representational restrictions: a zero latest value forces a zero prediction, and GELU constrains the range of multiplicative factors, limiting sign changes for standardized outcomes. Appendix F acknowledges zeros and missingness but does not demonstrate an implemented remedy or robustness analysis. These limitations are especially relevant to sparse gene expression and sales data and should be resolved before claiming broad applicability.

strengths: CLEF provides a simple, modular multiplicative forecasting decoder that can be attached to different sequence encoders. Its variable-wise factors permit direct, understandable manipulation of predicted values.

The evaluation is substantial: multiple application domains, matched CLEF/non-CLEF architectures, repeated seeds, distribution-shift experiments, and synthetic or semi-synthetic benchmarks with known counterfactual outcomes. Several comparisons show meaningful predictive gains.
The appendix supplies extensive experimental details, computational comparisons, and decoder ablations. The paper also acknowledges limitations involving missing values and zeros.
weaknesses: The causal justification is unsound as stated. Section 3.3 claims that separately encoding historical covariates and treatment makes representations treatment-invariant; this does not follow when historical covariates predict treatment assignment. Assumption 3.4 largely assumes the desired accurate counterfactual conditional mean rather than establishing it. Higher treatment-prediction BCE alone does not demonstrate balance without a well-trained held-out probe and an appropriate reference. Moreover, Tables 10–12 omit the no-balancing-loss models central to this claim and contain several decreases in BCE.

The central contribution is insufficiently distinguished from conditional forecasting with a multiplicative output parameterization. The 'temporal concept' is an endpoint ratio, not a rate of change or a trajectory representation with independently validated semantics. Direct prediction at a requested horizon is not unique to CLEF. The formulation ties intervention time to measurement time and does not establish general control over intervention onset and subsequent effects. Nor does the decoder enforce preservation of unaffected variables: it predicts a multiplier for every variable.

The cellular counterfactual benchmark does not establish intervention effects. Appendix C.1 constructs trajectories using optimal transport, assigns transcription-factor conditions retrospectively from differential expression between source and destination cell groups, and creates counterfactuals by resampling alternative continuations. This evaluates prediction of constructed, outcome-associated branches rather than responses to experimentally applied transcription-factor interventions. Original training trajectories and test counterfactuals also share exact prefixes; unseen interventions or independent biological counterfactual generalization are not established.

The clinical claims substantially exceed the evidence. The real patient datasets use diagnosis codes as conditions, rather than administered treatments. Manually halving a glucose-related multiplier and obtaining trajectories closer to non-diabetic patients does not identify an actionable treatment or validate causal downstream changes in white blood cells. The small case-study cohorts contain only 59 and 25 designated T1D patients. Additionally, Appendix C.2.3 treats ICD-9 category 250 as equivalent to type 1 diabetes, although that category includes multiple diabetes types; the control exclusion list also omits E10. These cohort definitions require correction or clarification.

The comparisons do not isolate the proposed explanation for the gains. SimpleLinear is persistence, not a fitted linear forecasting model, and persistence or VAR outperform neural methods on delayed WOT prediction. Missing comparisons include matched additive-residual decoders and strong direct horizon-conditioned predictors, alongside condition-removal or condition-shuffling ablations. The nine advertised baselines include several loss variants of only two counterfactual architectures. Table 9 also shows that adding intermediate steps improves WOT predictions, limiting the general argument that one-step prediction explains superior performance.

The decoder has consequential representational restrictions. Equation 3 forces a zero input coordinate to remain zero, while the GELU multiplier restricts negative ratios and therefore some sign-changing dynamics. These issues matter for sparse expression and sales data and standardized outcomes. Appendix F acknowledges zeros but does not quantify their prevalence or test remedies. Aggregate errors across clinical variables with different units also provide limited evidence that improvements are distributed across medically relevant measurements.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite extensive appendices: the supplied manuscript's code-release statements contain no visible repository URL. Dataset-split descriptions are also inconsistent: figure and table captions describe random cell/store splits, whereas Appendix C specifies start-cluster and state-based splits. The actual evaluation protocols need to be unambiguous.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful problem: conditioning multivariate trajectory predictions on future times and conditions, with applications across biology, healthcare, and sales.

CLEF is simple and modular. Its multiplicative decoder can be integrated with several sequence encoders and counterfactual prediction architectures with little additional parameter or computational overhead.

The empirical study is broad, including multiple datasets, three- or five-seed evaluations, distribution-shift experiments, decoder ablations, and synthetic counterfactual benchmarks. Improvements over corresponding neural baselines are substantial in several settings, particularly for patient distribution shifts and strongly confounded tumor simulations.
The appendix provides substantial detail on dataset construction, hyperparameters, computational costs, and experimental protocols.
weaknesses: The causal justification is unsound as stated. Section 3.3 claims that independently encoding covariates and treatments produces treatment-invariant representations, but covariates can remain predictive of treatment under confounding. Assumption 3.4 largely assumes the desired conditional-mean estimation property rather than establishing it. Higher treatment-prediction BCE alone does not demonstrate balance without a well-trained independent probe and an appropriate reference. Tables 10–12 also omit the unbalanced-loss variants central to this argument, and some CLEF variants have lower BCE than their baselines.

WOT-CF does not establish ground-truth intervention effects. Appendix C.1 constructs alternative futures by resampling optimal-transport trajectories and assigns transcription-factor conditions retrospectively from differential expression between source and destination cell groups. This tests prediction of alternative observational continuations, not whether activating a transcription factor causes the predicted trajectory. Training and test pairs also share their initial histories, and the split does not establish generalization to unseen interventions. The zero-shot counterfactual interpretation therefore exceeds the evidence.

The clinical conclusions are substantially stronger than the evaluation supports. Halving a predicted glucose value is not an identified clinical intervention, and increased similarity to selected controls does not establish physiological realism or beneficial treatment effects. The patient conditions are diagnosis codes rather than administered treatments. Cohort construction also needs correction or clarification: ICD-9 category 250 is not specific to type 1 diabetes, and the stated healthy-control exclusion list does not explicitly exclude E10. These issues undermine the claimed discovery of clinical interventions.

The novelty and baseline comparisons do not sufficiently isolate the contribution. The core mechanism is a learned per-variable multiplicative forecast relative to the latest observation; calling these factors temporal concepts does not itself establish a new interpretable representation. Missing comparisons include equally conditioned additive-residual and affine decoders and strong direct multi-horizon forecasting methods. SimpleLinear is effectively persistence, while VAR becomes numerically unstable on the clinical datasets. Improvements over the selected neural counterparts consequently do not establish the broad state-of-the-art claim.

The advertised timing and scope control are only partly demonstrated. The formulation ties intervention time to the prediction time, separated by a negligible interval, rather than independently varying intervention onset and outcome-measurement time. Direct prediction at a requested horizon is not unique to CLEF. Likewise, the decoder has no explicit mechanism enforcing unchanged values for unaffected variables; Table 5 shows prediction errors on such variables rather than guaranteed preservation.

The multiplicative decoder has consequential representational limitations. A zero-valued latest observation forces a zero prediction regardless of the condition, preventing zero-to-positive transitions relevant to gene expression and sales. GELU also restricts the attainable multipliers, which matters for signed or standardized outcomes. Appendix F acknowledges zeros and missingness, but proposes future remedies without demonstrating that the evaluated implementation resolves these problems.

The gains are not uniform: simple baselines outperform CLEF on delayed WOT prediction, and some delayed clinical comparisons favor the non-CLEF xLSTM. These results support a potentially useful forecasting inductive bias, but the unresolved causal claims, benchmark validity issues, and missing decisive ablations leave the paper below the acceptance threshold.
